weeks.summary: What is money, where does it come from, and why do we keep losing it on small things?
weeks.homework_summary: Track every rupee you spend for 3 days. No judgement — just see it.

lessons.title: What money actually is

content.intro: Money is just a tool — a way to swap things people make and do. Before money, people traded chickens for shoes. (Imagine carrying a chicken to the cinema.)

blocks.text: When you hold a ₹100 note, you're really holding a *promise* — a promise that other people will give you stuff worth ₹100 in exchange for it.
Money is value-stored-as-paper. Whoever controls how that paper is made controls a lot.

In this module you'll learn three big skills: how to make a budget that actually works, how to save without it feeling painful, and how to spot the difference between a smart investment and a bad bet.

content.key_takeaway: Money is a means, not an end. We earn it to buy choices.
content.mento_says: Hi! I'm Mento. Over the next 4 weeks, you'll go from 'I have no idea where my money goes' to 'I have a budget, a savings goal, and a paper portfolio.' One small step at a time.
content.story_hook: When India switched to UPI in 2016, a tea seller in a small Bihar village suddenly had the same payment system as a Fortune 500 company. Money is changing under your feet — and people who understand it win.
content.question: Right now, do you think of money more as 'a tool' or 'a goal'? Be honest.

lessons.coaching_moment: The first step to being good with money is realizing money is just a tool — not a goal. We use it to buy choices.

lessons.title: Money has 3 jobs (most people only know 1)

content.intro: Most people use money to spend. That's job #1. But money has two other jobs that almost nobody teaches in school.

cards.title: Job 1 — Spend
cards.body: Buys things now. Food, fuel, fun. Most people stop here.

cards.title: Job 2 — Save
cards.body: Sits and waits. Becomes your shield when life surprises you (it will).

cards.title: Job 3 — Grow
cards.body: Goes to work for you. Earns more money while you sleep — through interest, investing, or starting a side hustle.

content.key_takeaway: Adults who feel calm about money make all three jobs work — not just the spending one.
content.mento_says: If 100% of your money is on Job 1, you're playing on hard mode forever. Every rupee on Job 2 buys peace. Every rupee on Job 3 buys a future.

quiz.question: A friend says 'I'll just earn more next year — no need to save now'. What's the missing piece?
options: She's right — saving is for old people
She's only using Job 1; saving builds a shield against surprises
quiz.explanation: Earning more is great. But without Job 2 (Save) or Job 3 (Grow), one bad surprise wipes out every gain.

lessons.coaching_moment: Spend / Save / Grow. Memorize the trio. Most adults still only know one of them.

lessons.title: Needs vs Wants — the truth

content.intro: Most people *say* they know the difference between needs and wants. Most people are wrong — especially about themselves.

blocks.text: **Need**: you'd be in real trouble without it (food, shelter, school, basic clothes).
**Want**: it's nice to have, but you'd survive without it (a fancy phone, a third pair of shoes, that 4th milkshake this week).
Trick: ask yourself, 'will I still want this 30 days from now?' If you're not sure, it's a want.
Wants aren't bad — they're how we enjoy life. The trap is when we *call* a want a need so we don't feel guilty buying it.

examples.idea: NEED — your homework depends on it

examples.complaint: The newest model with RGB lights
A 5th pair of sneakers because the colour is nice
examples.idea: WANT — your feet only do one thing

content.story_hook: The richest 1% of people don't always spend the most. Many of them just got really, really good at telling needs from wants — and slowly invested the difference.

lessons.coaching_moment: A clear head about needs vs wants is the single biggest predictor of financial calm.

lessons.title: The BIG myths about money

content.intro: Movies, reels, and well-meaning relatives have filled your head with money myths. Most of them are wrong. Some are dangerous. Let's fix that.

myths.reality: Silence about money is how families stay confused for generations. The earlier you talk, the smarter your decisions get.

myths.myth: You need to be rich to start saving or investing.
myths.reality: ₹100/month invested at age 13 beats ₹1000/month invested at age 30 — over a lifetime. Time matters more than amount.

myths.myth: Smart people just 'know' how to handle money.
myths.reality: Money sense is a learned skill. Doctors and engineers go bankrupt all the time. School won't teach you this — you have to learn it on purpose.

myths.myth: If I earn more, I'll automatically save more.
myths.reality: Most people who get a raise immediately upgrade their lifestyle. Without a system, more income = more spending, not more savings.
Gambling is when the odds are against you on purpose. Investing is when you own a piece of something real that grows over time. They're opposites.

content.key_takeaway: Every myth you believe is a money leak. Patch them one by one.
content.mento_says: When a relative tells you something about money 'because that's how it's done', ask them WHY. Half the time, they'll realize they don't actually know.

lessons.coaching_moment: Most money mistakes aren't math errors — they're inherited beliefs nobody questioned.

lessons.title: Founder Spotlight: Falguni Nayar (Nykaa)

content.intro: You can read 100 finance books — but watching ONE real founder make smart money choices is worth more.

founder_spotlight.name: Falguni Nayar
founder_spotlight.story: She worked as an investment banker for 18 years before starting Nykaa at age 50. She knew exactly how money worked, saved methodically, and only then started her own company. When Nykaa went public in 2021, she became one of India's wealthiest self-made women.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Money sense first, big moves later. She didn't 'follow her dream' on day 1 — she got financially strong first, THEN took the risk.

blocks.text: Notice the order. Most movies show 'follow your passion → succeed.' Real life often goes 'understand money → save patiently → take a smart leap.'
You're 12-16. You don't need to start a company. You need to start understanding money — so when your moment comes, you're ready.

content.key_takeaway: Financial calm is built before the big risk, not after.

lessons.coaching_moment: The boring years of saving and learning ARE the journey. Don't skip them.

fields.hint: Pocket money, gifts, side hustle, allowance, festival cash — list them all.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you can't see where your money goes, you can't change it. This map is step zero.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Track every rupee for 3 days
lessons.summary: Step away from the screen. Track every single rupee that leaves your hand for the next 3 days.

content.intro: Mento needs FIELD evidence — not just notebook estimates. For the next 3 days, write down every rupee you spend, no matter how small. The ₹10 chips. The ₹30 auto. The ₹5 candy. ALL of it. Take a photo, voice note, or text — whichever is fastest. At the end, you'll see your spending in a way 95% of adults never have.

schema.brief: For 3 full days, log EVERY rupee that leaves your hand or wallet — no matter how small. Include UPI, cash, parental swipes for your stuff, the works.

lessons.coaching_moment: Don't try to spend 'better' during these 3 days. Spend exactly like you normally would. The truth is the prize.

lessons.title: Reflection: What did the truth feel like?

fields.name: biggest_surprise
fields.label: What's the biggest surprise from your 3-day track?
fields.hint: Was anything way more than you guessed? Way less?

fields.name: money_leaks
fields.label: Where did money leak that you didn't notice before?
fields.hint: Tiny repeated purchases are usually the answer.

fields.name: one_change
fields.label: One specific spending habit you'd change tomorrow
fields.hint: Be specific — 'I'll skip the daily ₹20 chips after school' beats 'I'll spend less.'

lessons.coaching_moment: Truth + small change = real progress. Don't try to overhaul everything — pick one leak and patch it.

weeks.title: Build Your First Budget
weeks.summary: Meet the 50/30/20 rule, the envelope method, and try running your own lemonade business to see budgeting come alive.
weeks.homework_summary: Run your pocket budget for one full week. Note where it broke.

lessons.title: The 50/30/20 rule

content.intro: There's no one perfect budget. But the 50/30/20 rule is a great starter, and it works at any income level — from a kid's pocket money to a CEO's salary.

blocks.text: **50%** of your money → needs (food, school, transport).
**30%** → wants (snacks, apps, fun).
**20%** → savings or paying off debts.
If your needs are eating more than 50%, that's a signal to look at recurring costs — not at squeezing fun.

content.key_takeaway: 50/30/20 is a starting point. Real life is messier. Adjust the numbers — but always keep a savings slice.
content.mento_says: If you're 14 and your 'needs' are 0 (parents cover them), bend the rule. Try 0/60/40 — most of your money is wants, but lock in 40% savings while you can.
content.story_hook: Senator Elizabeth Warren popularized 50/30/20 in a 2005 book she co-wrote with her daughter. It's now used by millions because it's simple enough to remember in a panic.

lessons.coaching_moment: Budgets aren't a punishment — they're a way to make sure your future self doesn't hate your present self.

lessons.title: The Envelope Method (a 100-year-old hack that still works)

content.intro: Before apps, before banks were everywhere, your great-grandmother probably used envelopes. It still works — and it's the BEST way to FEEL your budget instead of just thinking it.

cards.title: Step 1
cards.body: Write a category on each envelope: Food, Fun, Gifts, School, Savings.

cards.title: Step 2
cards.body: On payday (or pocket money day), put the planned ₹ amount in each envelope.

cards.title: Step 3
cards.body: When an envelope is empty, that category is DONE for the month. No borrowing from another envelope.

cards.title: Step 4
cards.body: Whatever's left in 'Savings' at month end → next month's savings or your goal jar.

content.key_takeaway: Envelopes work because they make spending visible. Apps hide; paper reveals.
content.mento_says: Yes, you can do this digitally with separate UPI labels or Paytm wallets. The point isn't paper — it's separation. Mixing all your money in one pile is the #1 reason budgets fail.

quiz.question: Why does 'no borrowing from another envelope' matter?
options: Once you start borrowing, the budget collapses — categories become meaningless
quiz.explanation: If you can borrow from Savings to fund Fun, Savings will always lose. Hard walls are what make a budget work.

lessons.coaching_moment: Envelopes turn budgeting from a thought into a feeling. That feeling is what changes habits.

lessons.title: Budget myths that wreck most people

content.intro: Why do most people give up on budgeting in 3 weeks? Because they believed one of these.

myths.myth: A real budget means tracking every single rupee in a spreadsheet.
myths.reality: The simplest budget you'll actually USE beats the perfect one you abandon. 5 categories is usually enough.
A budget INCLUDES fun (the 30%). It just stops fun from quietly eating your savings.

myths.myth: If I miss one day, the whole budget is broken.
myths.reality: Budgets are weekly averages, not daily perfection. Missing a day is normal — adjusting is the skill.

myths.myth: I'll start budgeting once I earn more.
myths.reality: If you can't manage ₹500/month, you won't suddenly manage ₹50,000/month. Habits scale; chaos scales faster.

content.key_takeaway: Most budget failures aren't math failures — they're belief failures.
content.story_hook: Studies show 60% of new budgets fail within 2 months. The ones that survive almost always start SIMPLE — 3-5 categories, not 30.

lessons.coaching_moment: If your budget feels like a prison, you've made it too tight. Loosen it; build the habit first.

lessons.title: How real Indian families actually budget

content.intro: Textbook budgets don't talk about Diwali bonuses, school fees due in March, the unexpected wedding gift, or the grandmother's sudden hospital visit. Real Indian household budgets do.

blocks.text: **The grandmother trick**: Many Indian families have an emergency fund hidden in cash, gold, or a separate FD that nobody touches except for emergencies. This is Job 2 (Save) at its cleanest.
**The festival fund**: Smart families set aside ₹500-2000/month for Diwali, Eid, Pongal, Christmas — so the festive season is JOY, not panic.
**School fee math**: Annual fees are predictable. Divide by 12 = monthly bucket. Treat it like a need, not a surprise.
What you can borrow from this: have a 'surprise fund' (even ₹100/month into a piggy bank counts).

content.key_takeaway: A budget that doesn't account for surprises ISN'T a budget. It's a wishlist.
content.mento_says: Talk to a parent or grandparent about how they handle festival expenses. You'll learn more in 5 minutes than from any finance influencer.

lessons.coaching_moment: Cultural context matters. Western 50/30/20 + Indian festival/family-cash logic = a budget that survives reality.

schema.intro: Use the 50/30/20 rule to split your monthly money. Try to land near 50/30/20 — but real budgets are messy. That's fine.

lessons.coaching_moment: Notice how hard it is to leave 20% for savings when fun feels urgent? That's the whole game.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Run your budget for a week
lessons.summary: Take the budget you just built and run it for 7 real days. Don't aim for perfect — aim for honest.

content.intro: A budget on paper is a hypothesis. A budget you've LIVED for a week is data. For the next 7 days, try to stick to your pocket budget. Each day, snap a quick text or voice note: 'today I stayed on budget' or 'I went over on Fun by ₹40 because of [reason]'.

schema.brief: Run your pocket budget for 7 days. Each day, log a quick check-in: did you stay on budget? If not, where did you go over and why?
persona_prompts: Day 7 review — what would you change?

lessons.coaching_moment: Going over budget isn't failure — it's data. The category that breaks first is usually the one with the wrong number on it.

fields.explanation: 20% is the savings/debt slice — it's what builds your future.

Banks give discounts for using envelopes

weeks.title: Save Smart, Spend Smarter
weeks.summary: Compound interest, splurge tests, and setting a savings goal you'll actually hit.
weeks.homework_summary: Track one 'splurge urge' you talked yourself out of this week.

lessons.title: Compound interest = magic

content.intro: Einstein supposedly called compound interest 'the eighth wonder of the world.' He probably didn't actually say it — but it doesn't matter. Compound interest IS that powerful.

blocks.text: Saving ₹100/month at 8% interest from age 12 → about ₹2,40,000 by age 25.
Saving the same ₹100/month from age 22 → only about ₹52,000 by age 25.
Same money. Same interest rate. **Different start age = 4.5x difference.**
Time is the secret ingredient. The earlier you start, the less effort it takes.

content.key_takeaway: Compound interest rewards TIME more than it rewards AMOUNT.
content.mento_says: Saving ₹50/week feels small. Compound interest disagrees. Your future self at 30 is begging you to start at 13.
content.story_hook: Warren Buffett, one of the richest people on earth, made 99% of his fortune AFTER his 50th birthday. Why? Because compound interest is exponential — the curve goes vertical late, but only if you start early.

lessons.coaching_moment: If you only remember one money lesson from this whole module: start early. Even small. Even now.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Your Compound Interest Calculator

schema.intro: Plug in your own numbers. Then plug in the same numbers but starting 5 years earlier. The gap will shock you.

fields.name: monthly_save
fields.label: How much can you save per month? (₹)
fields.hint: Start small — even ₹50 is fine.

fields.name: start_age
fields.label: What age would you start?

fields.name: end_age
fields.label: What age would you stop saving?

fields.name: estimated_total
fields.label: At 8% interest, what's your rough estimate? (₹)
fields.hint: It's OK to guess — the point is to get curious.

fields.name: actual_total
fields.label: Actual total (use any compound interest calculator online)
fields.hint: Search 'compound interest calculator' — most banks have one.

fields.name: surprise
fields.label: What surprised you?
fields.hint: Most people are shocked by how big the number gets — or how much earlier-starting matters.

lessons.coaching_moment: Numbers on paper hit harder than rules. Run this once and you'll never forget how powerful early saving is.

lessons.title: The splurge vs save test

content.intro: Every spend is a fork in the road: this thing now, or something bigger later? Three questions before any 'want' purchase.

blocks.text: **Question 1 — Will I care in 30 days?** If no, walk away. If you can't even remember what you wanted in a month, your future self definitely won't miss it.
**Question 2 — What's the next-best use of this money?** ₹500 spent on snacks is also ₹500 NOT spent on a book, a saving goal, or a friend's birthday gift. Compare.
**Question 3 — Am I bored / sad / tired?** If yes, sleep on it. Most splurges are emotional purchases dressed as needs.

content.key_takeaway: Saving isn't about deprivation — it's about funding what you actually care about.

examples.idea: Pause. Sales are ALWAYS happening. Decide cold, not hot.
Their wallet, your wallet. Different people, different goals.

examples.complaint: It's only ₹200, not a big deal
examples.idea: Six ₹200 'small deals' in a month = ₹1200. Watch the small ones.

lessons.coaching_moment: Most regret-purchases happen when you're tired, hungry, or scrolling at midnight. Sleep + sunlight = better spending.

lessons.title: Traps that quietly eat your savings

content.intro: Modern apps are designed to extract money from you in tiny, painless amounts. Tiny + frequent = huge totals. Here are the biggest traps.

myths.reality: ₹99/month = ₹1,188/year. Three of them = ₹3,564/year. Audit them every 3 months — most people forget half of theirs.

myths.myth: In-app purchases are different from real money.
myths.reality: Game coins, skins, and 'gems' cost the same rupees as anything else. Track them like real spend — because they ARE real spend.
Free trials become paid trials when you forget to cancel. Set a calendar reminder for the day BEFORE billing kicks in.

myths.myth: Delivery and convenience fees are tiny.
myths.reality: ₹40 delivery fee × 8 orders/month = ₹320/month = ₹3,840/year. Walk to the shop sometimes.

content.key_takeaway: It's not the big purchases that wreck most budgets — it's the tiny, repeating ones nobody notices.
content.mento_says: Open your phone. Go to Settings → Subscriptions. You'll find at least one you forgot about. That money is yours — go take it back.

lessons.coaching_moment: Modern apps are professionally designed to make spending feel painless. Make it visible again — that's how you escape the trap.

lessons.title: Saver Spotlight: Warren Buffett & Rakesh Jhunjhunwala

content.intro: Two of the greatest investors of our time. Both lived simply, saved relentlessly, and let time do the heavy lifting.

founder_spotlight.name: Rakesh Jhunjhunwala
founder_spotlight.story: Started investing in 1985 with ₹5,000. By the time he died in 2022, his net worth was over ₹40,000 crore. He didn't 'pick lucky stocks' — he stayed in the market for 37 years through every crash, every recovery, every panic.
founder_spotlight.lesson: TIME in the market beats TIMING the market. Boring patience beats exciting trades.

blocks.text: Warren Buffett, age 94, still lives in the same Omaha house he bought in 1958. He drives himself. He eats McDonald's. He gave away most of his fortune.
What both men have in common: they don't spend like rich people. They invest like rich people. Big difference.

content.key_takeaway: Wealth isn't built by spending it. It's built by NOT spending it for a long time.

lessons.coaching_moment: When you see luxury influencers, remember — many of the actual wealthy are quiet, patient, and bored on purpose.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Set a real savings goal

schema.intro: A goal without a number and a date is a wish. Make this real.

fields.name: goal_thing
fields.label: What are you saving for?
fields.hint: Be specific — 'new running shoes', not 'something cool'.

fields.name: goal_amount
fields.label: How much will it cost? (₹)

fields.name: monthly_save
fields.label: How much can you save each month? (₹)
fields.hint: Be honest — small numbers are fine.

fields.name: goal_date
fields.label: When do you want to hit your goal?

lessons.coaching_moment: A goal you can name, count, and date is a goal you can hit. Vague wishes don't survive.

lessons.title: Field Mission: Catch one splurge urge
lessons.summary: This week, watch yourself want something — and don't buy it. Document the urge.

content.intro: The next time you feel a sudden 'I need this NOW' urge — pause. Don't buy. Wait at least 24 hours. Document the urge: what you wanted, why, what time of day, your mood. Then check in 24 hours later: do you still want it? This is the splurge muscle. The more you train it, the more financial freedom you build.

schema.brief: Notice ONE 'I want this NOW' urge this week. DON'T buy it. Wait 24 hours. Then log: did you still want it? What did the urge feel like at the time vs after?
persona_prompts: Why I wanted it (mood, context, time of day)
After 24 hours — did I still want it?

lessons.coaching_moment: Catching one urge is enough. The point isn't to never buy fun things — it's to know the difference between 'I want this' and 'I think I want this'.

lessons.title: Reflection: Your one money rule

fields.name: rule_one
fields.label: One money rule I will live by from now on
fields.hint: Make it concrete and easy to remember. e.g. 'Never buy anything over ₹500 without sleeping on it.'

fields.name: why_this
fields.label: Why this rule, for me, right now?
fields.hint: What habit is it fixing?

fields.name: share_with

fields.hint: Saying it out loud makes it real.

lessons.coaching_moment: A rule written down and shared with one person is worth ten thoughts you keep to yourself.

weeks.homework_summary: Pick 3 imaginary stocks and follow them for a week.

lessons.title: Risk and return — they come together

content.intro: Anything that promises high return with no risk is either a scam or a misunderstanding. There are no exceptions.

cards.title: Low risk → low return
cards.body: Bank savings, fixed deposits. You won't lose, but you won't grow much either. ~3-7%/year.

cards.title: Medium risk → medium return
cards.body: Bonds, index funds. They wobble but tend up over years. ~8-12%/year.

cards.title: High risk → high return (or loss)
cards.body: Individual stocks, crypto. Big swings either way. Could be +50% or -50% in a year.

content.key_takeaway: Match the risk to the goal. Money you need in 6 months ≠ money you won't touch for 10 years.
content.mento_says: Anyone promising you 'guaranteed 30% returns' is selling you something. Real investing is boring on purpose — boring is the price of safe.
content.story_hook: In 2008, the world's stock markets dropped 50%+ in a few months. People who stayed in and added more money over the next 10 years grew their wealth 3x. People who panicked and sold locked in losses forever.

lessons.coaching_moment: Don't avoid risk. Match it to your time horizon.

lessons.title: What is a stock, really?

content.intro: A stock isn't a number on a screen. It's a tiny slice of a real, working company. When you buy 1 share of TCS, you OWN a microscopic piece of TCS.

blocks.text: If TCS makes more profit, your slice is worth more. If TCS struggles, your slice is worth less. That's the whole game.
Stock PRICE moves up and down every minute based on what people THINK TCS is worth — but the underlying COMPANY changes much more slowly.
Buy a piece of a company you understand and would still own if the screen went blank for 5 years.

content.key_takeaway: You're buying a slice of a real business — not betting on a number.

quiz.question: If you buy 10 shares of a company, you own…
options: 10 lottery tickets that pay if the price goes up
A tiny but real share of that company's future profits
A debt the company owes you
quiz.explanation: Shares = ownership. As the company grows, your share grows. You're a tiny part-owner, not a gambler.

lessons.coaching_moment: Investing is buying business ownership at a sale price. Trading is guessing tomorrow's mood. Different games.

lessons.title: Why diversification works

content.intro: Don't put all your eggs in one basket. Yes, your grandparent already said this. They were right.

blocks.text: If you put 100% of your savings into ONE stock and that company has a bad year, you're in big trouble.
If you spread it across 10 different things — different industries, different countries, different sizes — one bad apple barely shows up.
Diversification isn't about being timid. It's about making sure no single mistake can wreck you.

examples.complaint: All my money in one tech stock
examples.idea: If tech crashes, you lose everything. High risk, no buffer.

examples.complaint: Money spread across 10 stocks in 5 industries
examples.idea: If 1 crashes, the others can absorb. You stay in the game.

examples.complaint: Index fund (which IS hundreds of stocks)
examples.idea: Instant diversification with one purchase. Why most experts recommend it for beginners.

content.key_takeaway: Spreading risk is what lets you stay in the game long enough for compounding to work.

lessons.coaching_moment: Diversification isn't sexy. It's just the difference between staying rich and going back to zero.

lessons.title: Investment myths that cost real money

content.intro: Most beginner investors lose money in the first year. Almost always because of one of these myths.

myths.myth: I can pick winners by reading the news.
myths.reality: By the time news is news, the price has already moved. News-based trading is a famous beginner mistake.

myths.myth: If a stock is going up, it'll keep going up.
myths.reality: Stocks revert to fair value. Hot stocks often crash; ignored stocks often quietly grow. The opposite of intuition.

myths.myth: If I lose money on a stock, I should hold until it 'comes back'.
myths.reality: Many stocks NEVER come back. Sometimes selling at a loss frees money for better opportunities.
You can start with ₹100 in an index fund SIP today. Time matters more than starting amount — see Week 3.

myths.myth: Crypto / meme stocks are an easy way to get rich fast.
myths.reality: For every 1 person who got rich, 100 lost everything. Survivorship bias is real. The stories you hear are filtered.

content.key_takeaway: Investing rewards patience and skepticism. Most 'hot tips' are how you lose money politely.
content.mento_says: If a friend says 'this stock is going to the moon', that's not advice — that's hype. Real investing is calm, slow, and almost always boring.

lessons.coaching_moment: The riskiest thing you can do as a new investor is FEEL CERTAIN. Stay humble — markets humble everyone.

lessons.title: Founder Spotlight: Nithin Kamath (Zerodha)

content.intro: Most Indians who invest in stocks today use Zerodha. The story of how it was built is also a story about money discipline.

founder_spotlight.name: Nithin Kamath
founder_spotlight.story: Started trading at 17. Lost most of his money in 2001. Spent the next 9 years carefully learning. In 2010, he founded Zerodha — built it slowly, with no outside investors, no marketing budget. Today it's India's largest stockbroker, profitable from day one, with no debt.
founder_spotlight.lesson: Lose early, learn deeply, build patiently. He's said: 'The best money lesson is being broke once. You never forget.'

blocks.text: Notice what he didn't do: chase trends, take huge risks, raise giant funding. Notice what he did: study, save, build slowly.
Many of India's quietest billionaires share this pattern. The flashy ones often go bust.

content.key_takeaway: In investing AND in business, slow + skeptical + patient outlasts fast + confident + loud.

lessons.coaching_moment: Smart investors aren't the ones with the most exciting stories. They're the ones still around 30 years later.

lessons.title: Worksheet: Build a paper portfolio

schema.intro: Pretend you have ₹10,000 to invest. Build a diversified imaginary portfolio. Pick 5-10 different things across different industries. You're not actually buying — just practicing the THINKING.

fields.name: stock_1
fields.label: Investment 1 — name + ₹ amount + industry
fields.hint: e.g. 'Reliance — ₹1500 — Energy/Telecom'

fields.name: stock_2
fields.label: Investment 2 — name + ₹ amount + industry

fields.name: stock_3
fields.label: Investment 3 — name + ₹ amount + industry

fields.name: stock_4
fields.label: Investment 4 — name + ₹ amount + industry

fields.name: stock_5
fields.label: Investment 5 — name + ₹ amount + industry

fields.name: industries
fields.label: List the industries you covered. Are any duplicated? (Diversification check)
fields.hint: e.g. 2 tech + 1 bank + 1 FMCG + 1 energy

fields.name: why_these
fields.label: Why these 5? Pick the ONE you understand best — explain it in 1 sentence.
fields.hint: If you can't explain why you'd own it, you probably shouldn't.

lessons.coaching_moment: If your 5 picks are all in 1 or 2 industries, that's not diversification — that's a concentration bet. Spread wider.

lessons.title: Stock Street — paper trade for a week
lessons.game_purpose: Practice picking, holding, and letting go without real money on the line.
lessons.coaching_moment: Notice your gut on a 10% drop. That feeling is the most important data you'll ever collect.

lessons.title: Reflection: Your money pledge

fields.name: rule_one
fields.label: One money rule I will live by from now on
fields.hint: Make it concrete and easy to remember.

fields.name: first_save
fields.label: First thing I'll save for (₹ amount + name)

fields.name: trap_to_avoid
fields.label: One money trap I'm going to avoid
fields.hint: Be honest — what trips you up most?

fields.name: investing_starter
fields.label: If I were to start a tiny SIP one day, what would my first ₹500/month go into?
fields.hint: Imaginary is fine — practice the choice.

fields.name: share_with
fields.label: One person I'll share this pledge with

lessons.coaching_moment: A pledge written down and shared with one person is worth ten thoughts you keep to yourself.

lessons.title: Final Money Mastery Quiz

fields.question: Highest expected return generally comes with…
fields.explanation: Risk and return move together. There's no free lunch.

fields.question: Diversification means…
fields.explanation: Spread = no single failure can wreck you.

fields.question: If you'll need money in 6 months, where should it MOST likely be?

options.label: In a savings account or short-term FD

fields.question: What does the 50/30/20 rule do best?
fields.explanation: It's a starter budget, not an investment formula.

fields.question: Why does compound interest favor early starters?
A common SAVING TRAP that quietly drains money is…
fields.explanation: Tiny repeating charges (subscriptions, in-app buys, delivery fees) silently eat budgets. Audit them.

fields.question: Owning a share of a company means…

options.label: You're betting on a price number
You own a tiny piece of a real business

fields.explanation: Stock = ownership in a real company. The price moves; the underlying business is what actually matters.

lessons.coaching_moment: You've just covered what most adults wish they'd learned at your age.

points: Risk and return come together — no free lunch
A stock = a slice of a real business, not a number on a screen
Diversification keeps you in the game when one bet goes wrong
Investment myths (hot tips, news-trading, crypto-fast-rich) cost real money
Patience + skepticism + time = the true investor's edge
week_recap.try_this: Pick ONE listed company you actually use products from (e.g. Maruti, HDFC, Zomato). Read 2 articles about it. Notice — when you understand a company, the stock price feels less scary.
